### Book Binding and Identification

The volume is bound in aged parchment, also known as vellum <note>high-quality writing surface made from specially prepared animal skin</note>. The front cover shows signs of heavy use, including a large stain and small punctures where leather ties or metal clasps would have once kept the book tightly closed. 

Identification marks have been added to the exterior in two places: hand-written directly onto the top edge of the pages, and on a printed paper label affixed to the spine.

# Here begin the fables

Column 1:

They lost their own things while they sought what belonged to another. <note>original: "Perdiderunt propria dum alienum appetunt"; this is the classic moral of the Dog and the Shadow.</note>
A dog was carrying meat across a river, and so forth.
<margin>Of the wolf and the lamb</margin>
It is said that a wolf and a lamb were thirsty at the same stream.
The wolf accused the lamb because he had muddied the water.
Indeed, the rights and faithfulness of prayers <note>original: "precum"; this may be a scribal variation of "pretium" (price) or "probi" (the upright)</note> were lost in truth.
Having first convicted him, the wolf killed the lamb with his jaws.
<margin>Of the wolf and the crane</margin>
To the wolf, a bone he had devoured was stuck in his throat.
He asked the crane with a prayer and a price <note>original: "prece pretioque"; a medieval legal idiom meaning "by begging and bribery."</note>.
The long neck of the crane extracted it from the throat.
<margin>Of the wolf and the dog</margin>
From the wolf's throat, teeth were pressing the wolf. <note>Likely referring to the wolf's hunger or the threat of the dog's bite.</note>
A dog, full of meat, was walking in the field.
The weak and very fearful wolf followed the dog.
For a long time, though the dog was well-off, the wolf overcame him. <note>The wolf chooses hunger and freedom over the dog's collar and steady food.</note>
<margin>Of the mouse and the frog</margin>
The frog was dragging the mouse because it was an aquatic creature.
The mouse was unwilling, but bound by a cord, he held on.
A kite <note>term: "milvus"; a common medieval bird of prey similar to a hawk.</note> snatched the mouse and killed the frog too.
<margin>Of the wolf and the sheep</margin>
The wolf in the grove thus warned the sheep-dweller:
That the sheep had come into the pastures through the groves.
<margin>Of the dog and the sheep</margin>
The dog begged the sheep for bread.
A vulture, a wolf, and a kite bear witness.
The sheep, having been sworn against, gave back the loaves.
<margin>Of the puppy and the little donkey</margin>
The donkey saw the puppy being pampered.
The donkey himself wished to be pampered like the puppy.
Struck with a rope, the dog <note>The text says "canis" (dog), but the fable usually describes the donkey being driven back.</note> was driven back to the stable.
<margin>Of the lion and the mouse</margin>
A lion lay sleeping in his lair.
A mouse began to run over the lion's head.
The lion caught the mouse and let it go alive.
Later, the lion lay bound in a rope.
The lion filled the forest with the sound of his greatness.
The mouse came to him and began to gnaw the ropes.
<margin>Of the kite and the dove</margin>
The kite deceived the dove with prayer and fraud.
Once peace was made, he ate the dove again.
<margin>Of the vulture</margin>
The vulture sent some birds to the banquets.
He killed all the birds by prayer and price.
<margin>Of the dog and the heir</margin>
A dog saw his master thus placed at death.
He lay by the master's side with the coins.
<margin>Of the peacock</margin>
The peacock asked the dove with prayer and price:
That the peacock wished to become king of the doves.
The dove by no means allowed the peacock to do this.

<column-break/>

Column 2:

<margin>Of the fox and the raven</margin>
The fox saw the bread in the raven's hand <note>original: "manu"; used here for the raven's grip or beak.</note> secretly.
He praised the raven so that he might give his voice.
The raven, raising his voice, lost the bread.
<margin>Of the aged lion</margin>
The lion reached old age, and the donkey spoke thus.
The donkey fiercely struck the lion with his tooth.
The lion said this: "Base ones mock me as if I were dead."
<margin>Of the mouse and the mouse</margin>
A mouse from the city came to another mouse.
Thus he led the mouse from the country to the city.
The country mouse fears the city that gives bread.
<margin>Of the eagle and the tortoise</margin>
The tortoise asked the eagle with prayer and price:
That the tortoise might be a flying thing above the clouds.
The eagle let go of the tortoise over the rocks.
The tortoise left many fragments on the rock.
<margin>Of the fox and the stork</margin>
The fox invited the stork to a meal of bread.
He spread the food across the flat marble.
The stork invited the fox to meat.
She kept the meat in a narrow-necked jar.
<margin>Of Juno and the peacock</margin>
The peacock asked Juno with prayer and price:
That she might preserve the appearance and voice of the peacock.
Juno prepared a very sweet response for the peacock.
<margin>Of the panther</margin>
A panther lay thus having fallen into a pit.
The peasants pelted her with stones to the injury of death.
The shepherds saved her for life.
The panther ravages men and cattle through the fields.
The panther spared the cattle of the shepherds.
<margin>Of the country and the city</margin>
The country mouse was thus called by the city mouse.
The city gives rich foods; in the country, he had nothing.
Flee from the country, mouse; a fugitive mouse in the night.
<margin>Of the lion and the mouse</margin>
The same mouse well served his master and the rope.
<margin>Of the dog and the dog</margin>
A dog asked another dog for a place to give birth.
The first dog did not want to return the place to its master.
<margin>Of the stag and the spring</margin>
A stag saw his horns in a spring.
The stag despised his thin legs.
In the grove, the stag was overcome because of his horns.
His nimble legs saved the stag from death.
<margin>Of the fox and the grape</margin>
The fox prepared himself to reach high for the grape.
The fox said that the grape was sour.
<margin>Of the weasel</margin>
A weasel asked a man for its life:
Because the master's house was weighed down by many mice.
The master did not wish to save her life.

### There are thirty kinds of fools

<note>This section is translated from Old French. It is a satirical list of "fools" common in medieval wisdom literature.</note>

He who has no one to serve him, yet ought not to serve.
He who runs everywhere and receives nothing.
He who **threatens** so much that no one fears him.
He who **speaks** so much that no one listens.
He who swears [oaths] so much that no one believes him.
He who expects gratitude from a **child** or a **drunkard**.
He who always bargains and has nothing in his purse.
He who trusts his enemy.
He who listens to the doubt? and helps no one.
He who desires much and adds nothing.
He who gets himself drunk to get others drunk.
He who promises much and has nothing to give.
He who hates everyone and no one loves him.
He who <unclear>...</unclear> can endure nothing.
He who drives away his own people for a **stranger**.
He who asks for a thing he does not have.
He who gets angry where he has no power.
He who offends God and acts the most.
He who plays too much with his lord.
He who knows his own harm and does nothing to stop it.
He who loves higher than he can reach.
He who speaks of love only when it is asked of him.
He who swears by the thing that caused him harm.
He who trusts too much in his own greed.
He who puts himself in **danger** without having the strength for it.
He who loses his own good for the sake of another’s.
He who brings shame on himself through another’s anger.
He who blames another for what he himself is guilty of.
He who thinks to bring down a heart by starving it.

<vocab>fools (stultorum), types (genera), He who (Ki/Qui), threatens (menace), speech (parōle)</vocab>

### On the purification of common salt and salt gems
Take these as the labor requires: grind them <unclear>on the ground</unclear> and dissolve them in four parts of rainwater. Distill through a woolen filter <note>original: "filtro lani"; a common method of straining liquids through wool or felt to remove impurities.</note>. Once boiled, it remains in the vessel until the salt coagulates. Remove the dregs; dry and grind <unclear>the salt</unclear>. Repeat this by placing it in a jar, sealing it with clay <note>original: "lutum luto"; likely refers to 'Lute of Hermes,' a clay sealant used to make vessels airtight.</note>, and purifying it. Afterward, dissolve the salt again in four times its weight of water, distill through the filter, and coagulate it. Perform this until the salt is purified as you know how. <unclear>...</unclear>

### On the purification of alkali salt, that is, the salt which is extracted from glass
$\lceil$ Take alkali salt or alkali alum; grind the whole and place it in six parts of rainwater. Let it soak for three days, stirring it three times a day so it dissolves well. Distill through a filter, coagulate, and perform this three times as described above. Dry it until the red color <note>original: "rubeis"; the appearance of a red tint often signaled a change in the chemical state or the presence of specific impurities.</note> no longer falls from it.

### ¶ On the preparation of urine.

<meta>This page continues the laboratory instructions from the previous section. While the previous page focused on the "first water" and the assaying of metals like lead and silver, this page provides a collection of recipes for preparing various chemical "waters" (distilled acids and solvents) and purified salts. These are the foundational reagents necessary for the more complex metallurgical work described earlier.</meta>

# Method of preparing mineral water

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take 2 pounds of quicksilver <term>Mercurius vivus: liquid mercury</term>, and 2 pounds each of vitriol and burnt alum. Let all be mixed together upon a marble slab; then add water so that you may capture its essence <note>original: "extremitatem ejus," referring to the most potent part or distillate</note>. Then place it in another vessel by the neck, and thus it distills into the receiver over a fire.

## Method of preparing common salt

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take 1 pound of living salt <note>likely unrefined sea salt</note>, 1 pound of purified quicklime <term>calcis vive: calcium oxide, a caustic substance made by heating limestone</term>, 3 ounces of rock salt <term>salis gemmi: pure mineral salt or halite</term>, and 2 ounces of alkali salt. Let the powder be ground by itself, which you shall place upon marble in the sun so that salt may be formed within the powder.

## Method of preparing sal ammoniac

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take 1 pound of living salt, 1 pound of lime, half a pound of saltpeter <note>original: "salis nitri"</note>, and four ounces of calcined vitriol. Let them be ground and raised <note>original: "levantur," likely referring to the process of sublimation where the salt is heated until it rises as a vapor and solidifies at the top of the vessel</note> by fire.

## Method of preparing aqua fortis in a simple way

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take equal parts of vitriol and saltpeter <note>original: "salis petri"</note>. Let both be ground very finely like lentils <note>original: "lenticulatim," meaning to a very fine, granular consistency</note> near the fire. Once mixed, let it distill into water through an alembic <term>limbecum: a specialized glass or ceramic still used for distillation</term>; then let it distill by itself and be macerated through twenty cycles <note>original: "vias viges"</note>.

## Method of preparing aqua fortis in different ways

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take 3 pounds of vitriol, 12 ounces of saltpeter, 12 ounces of burnt alum, and 3 ounces of Armenian stone <term>lapis armeni: a blue copper carbonate mineral, often azurite, used here as a catalyst or reagent</term>. Let the vitriol and saltpeter be mixed in equal parts. Then, with two liquid parts, make this water. Then add four ounces of other "mineral salt of life." Let this be burned over wood in such a manner; it thus possesses the greatest power by itself for purifying quicksilver.

## Method of preparing salt

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take 2 pounds of quicklime, 10 pounds of ash, and 3 ounces of vitriol. Let them be boiled in common water—using plenty of hot and clear water. Then let this be filtered through a <unclear>cloth</unclear> or linen. Then take the clear water and make it evaporate over a fire until the appearance of salt comes to the surface. Let it sit in a vessel in the cold; then you will find salt as clear as ice. As for saltpeter, purify it by itself, or as was said above regarding the purification of common salt. Do everything so that the salt is purified, namely through water or cold, that is, through the bag <note>original: "peram," likely a conical filter bag</note>, etc.

## Preparation of <unclear>wrinkle-clearing</unclear> water

℞ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take 15 pounds of clear spring or river water, 10 pounds of clear honey, and half a pound of vitriol. Create the water in a glass vessel and let it stand clear in the sun. The water adds calcination and colors to the vitriol; then it occupies other clear pounds as you will see written below. And it should be known that the honey must always be purified, otherwise it does not receive its power as is seen in practice, etc.

-> In this manner <-

It is not enough for a doctor to be made <note>likely referring to the training or skill required to use these substances</note>; it has power through the heat and dryness of the humors, and for longevity, these things are done. ### Preparation of fixed Arsenic

<unclear>Fix the Arsenic with purified saltpeter <note>original: "sale nitri"</note> by distilling it in a moist state through a retort so that it becomes "strong water" <note>original: "aqua fortis," a corrosive mineral acid, usually nitric acid</note>.</unclear>
<unclear>Then let the distilled Arsenic be fixed in a glass vessel into a red or white color, and this water</unclear>
<unclear>from the Retort is the best.</unclear>

### Preparation of alkali salt

<unclear>Alkali salt <term>sal alkali: a basic salt, often potash or soda, used as a flux in melting metals</term> is made from the ashes of plants; take all the moist parts in a cucurbit <note>the lower part of a distilling apparatus</note> which you have</unclear>
<unclear>purified, and above let hot water be filtered, and thus through distillation and drying, the gall <note>vitriol or mineral essence</note> is produced.</unclear>
<unclear>In this way, the alkali salt remains at the bottom, dried into a single "mastery" <note>a concentrated or perfected substance</note></unclear>
<unclear>which is at its strongest in this fixed gall.</unclear>

### Preparation of saltpeter

<unclear>Saltpeter <note>original: "Sal nitrum"</note> is to be distilled and dried into a gall; this is done when this salt is made to enter</unclear>
<unclear>the gall so that it passes through and [becomes fixed].</unclear>

### Preparation of pure Vitriol

<unclear>Pure Vitriol <term>vitriolum: a sulfate of a metal, like iron or copper, often called 'the green lion'</term> is distilled in purified tartar; let it be purified and taken away from the "dead head" <note>original: "ex mortuo," the dregs left in the vessel after distillation</note></unclear>
<unclear>of the vessel in which the distillation is performed; repeat this as many times as needed, then thus by</unclear>
<unclear>distillation and it is made solid.</unclear>

### Preparation and sublimation of Mercury

<unclear>Purify and distill Mercury from quicklime <note>original: "calce viva"</note>; then put the matter <note>original: "mory," likely a shorthand for 'materia' or 'mercurii'</note> into the quicklime</unclear>
<unclear>in a dry state, thus a pure dry substance is produced from the dry, fixed matter. In the vessel of death <note>the bottom of the still</note></unclear>
<unclear>the matter is appropriated at the bottom and thus it becomes a dry Mercury,</unclear>
<unclear>the whitest possible; let this be done where the water above is closed in the concave edge of the vessel</unclear>
<unclear>with the pure matter under a gentle heat, which will be made by the light until all of it is fixed and thus</unclear>
<unclear>congealed. In the pure dry state, let the whole thing be made from the salt under a gentle heat, both pure and the matter.</unclear>

### Preparation and sublimation of sulfur

<unclear>Boil Sulfur in this water from the fixed matter, and then in this way let the moist</unclear>
<unclear>pure part be made under a gentle heat; then let the fixed matter from the pure part be made again into a pure</unclear>
<unclear>bronze-like substance; afterward it is said that this salt becomes white, living, and dry.</unclear>

### Preparation of the sublimate of gold

<unclear>Gold <note>original: "Aurũ"</note> is distilled in strong water <note>aqua fortis</note> and distilled; then it is dried at the bottom and thus supported</unclear>
<unclear>as a thing from the white and fixed matter of sulfur.</unclear>

### Preparation and fixation of the nitre of Antimony

<unclear>Fix the dissolved substance at the bottom of the pure matter with a gentle heat; the fixed matter becomes pure and then fixed,</unclear>
<unclear>and thus pure in the retort; let the matter be pure so that it is sublimated; thus close it purely.</unclear>

### Preparation of the white and red waters

<unclear>Take living mercury <note>quicksilver</note> which is a hot matter, and it will be made like the "light of the red" <note>a high-level alchemical stage</note> matter;</unclear>
<unclear>being dried, let it be sublimated and thus closed so that it is like the matter of the pure matter.</unclear>

<unclear>the matter with the water is clarified and distilled in glass; thus it is produced</unclear>
<unclear>from the water and thus the red sublimate with the matter of the gentle water.</unclear>

### Concerning the preparation of saltpeter

<unclear>matter is placed above; afterward, it becomes gall again, which is called the dry</unclear>
<unclear>gentle matter. It is made pure, and afterward, the pure matter is called the water, and thus distitll it;</unclear>

### Concerning the cleansing and preparation of alkali salt

<unclear>Alkali salt is purified from hot water and galls, and then closed, and then made again from that</unclear>

### Concerning the cleansing and preparation of sal ammoniac

<unclear>Sal ammoniac <note>original: "Sal armoniaũ," ammonium chloride</note> is so called; put it in pure water and filter it. The moist matter</unclear>

<unclear>pure substance be placed above and thus closed from the matter.</unclear>

### Concerning the preparation and processing of mercury

### Concerning the preparation and cleansing of nitre

<unclear>In the gentle water from the matter, it is dried with the pure matter; thus the pure matter is</unclear>

### Concerning the preparation of talc and its processing

<unclear>Talc <note>often referring to mica or any shimmering mineral</note> is supported in a dry state by the pure matter; it is made into three parts.</unclear>
<unclear>The matter in the water is said to be from the white water; thus it is made gentle and dried.</unclear>
<unclear>The pure water is dried again, and thus the matter becomes white; thus with pure and gentle water,</unclear>
<unclear>it is dried in the dry state; thus the pure water and the matter are made pure.</unclear>

## On the synthesis of mercury
<note>original: "De syncrasione mercurij"</note>

Take Mercury as much as you wish: purify it twice together: and with a part of common salt <note>original: "salis cōi" (salis communis)</note>: at a weight of 1 to 3: for the part of Mercury. <meta>The previous page discussed alchemical processes like the calcination of metals and the use of "strong waters" for refining silver. This page shifts abruptly from laboratory practice to scholastic metaphysics, specifically debating the philosophical definition of the soul (anima) and how it fits into the Aristotelian categories of substance and being.</meta>

### Book 1

To the 1st [objection] I say that although within the category <term>category: or "genus," a fundamental classification of things in Aristotelian logic</term> of substances there is something "first" which is **pure act** <note>original: *actus purus*; a philosophical term for a being with no unfulfilled potential, traditionally identifying God.</note>, it is nonetheless not required for a thing to have the nature of such a "first principle" simply to belong to that category. For something to be in a category, it is sufficient that it be composed of **essence and being** <note>original: *essentia et esse*</note> or that it possesses some characteristic of the category. Therefore, although the soul does not have the nature of "pure act," it is still in the category of substance because it is an **incomplete substance**; just as matter, which does not have the nature of the "first principle," is still within a category. The argument therefore proceeds from the "first" in a category insofar as it is the ideal example, not simply as it exists within that category.

---

To the 2nd I say that this [argument] proceeds from the "first" in a category which is the cause of others in that same category. Such a thing is something that possesses every perfection of that category. This is said to be "first" in the category not because it is first in the order of <unclear>perfection</unclear> or <unclear>generation</unclear>, but because it serves as the **rule** <note>i.e., the standard of measurement</note> for others. Hence, it is not required for it to be "pure act," but it is sufficient that it possesses the maximum perfection of that category, as is evident in other categories.

---

To the 3rd I say that although the soul does not have every perfection of a substance, it does have the perfection of an **incomplete substance**. Thus, it is in the category of substance not as a "species" <note>a specific type of independent thing</note>, but as the **principle of a species** <note>a component part that defines what a species—like a human being—is</note>. Therefore, although it is not in the category *primarily* by itself, it is nevertheless in the category *secondarily* by itself, or it belongs to the category **reductively** <note>meaning it is categorized by its relationship to the whole human being</note>, as **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian</note> says in the *Summa Theologiae*, part 1, question 75, article 4, reply to the 2nd objection.

---

To the 4th I say that although the soul does not have matter, it nevertheless has something **similar to matter**, namely **potency** <term>potency: the capacity to become something or receive a quality, as opposed to "act" which is the fulfillment of that capacity</term>. Thus, it is said to be composed of **potency and act**, or of **essence and being**, as **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose work *De Hebdomadibus* explored how things are good</note> says in his *De Hebdomadibus* and **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note> in chapter 4 of *The Divine Names*. In this way, the soul is not entirely simple <note>In scholasticism, "simple" means having no parts or divisions.</note>.

---

To the 5th I say that although the soul is not in a place **by itself** <note>original: *per se*</note>, it is nevertheless in a place **by accident** <note>original: *per accidens*; meaning indirectly, by virtue of its connection to something else</note>, specifically through the body to which it is united. Hence, although it is not moved by itself, it is moved by accident according to the movement of the body. Furthermore, for something to be in a category, it is not required that it be in a place *by itself*; it is sufficient that it be in a place in some manner, as is evident regarding **angels**.

---

<meta>This page marks a sharp transition in the manuscript. While the previous page concludes a philosophical discussion on the nature of the soul and virtue, page 53 begins a series of practical alchemical recipes (labeled "Art: 154" and following). This suggests the volume is a "commonplace book" where a scholar or practitioner recorded diverse knowledge, ranging from metaphysics to laboratory chemistry.</meta>

### Art: 154

Take a **mineral stone** <note>original: *lapid: mineralem*</note> and grind it upon a **marble slab** <note>original: *marmore*; marble was preferred for grinding as it did not react easily with chemicals</note>, and grind it very well into a powder; grind it by itself for **three days and nights** until it is **impalpable** <term>impalpable: a powder so fine that the grains cannot be felt between the fingers</term>. Then place it in a glass vessel and let **spring water** be poured over it while warm. Let it sit in a pot over a fire for 3 days, and then **distill it through an alembic** <term>alembic: a traditional alchemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube for distilling liquids</term>. That which remains in the bottom, grind again with spring water and distill...

<margin>1</margin> Grind **rock salt** <note>original: *salis gemmae*; literally "salt of the gem," referring to pure halite</note> and **common salt** in spring water and let it be dissolved; afterwards, distill it through an alembic and let it be saved. Do the same with **vitriol** <term>vitriol: a term for metallic sulfates, like copper or iron sulfate, used for making acids</term>, **saltpeter** <note>original: *salis nitri*</note>, and **alkali salt**.

<margin>2</margin> Take **powdered sulfur** and put it over the fire in a newly **leaded pot**; then let **oil of tartar** <note>original: *oleum tataricum*; a solution of potassium carbonate</note> be poured over it. Place it in a damp place for 3 days and let it be **sublimated** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then cools back into a solid, used for purification</term>; let it become an oil.

<margin>3</margin> And do thus with all **bodies** <note>original: *corporibus*; in alchemy, this usually refers to the seven metals</note> and thus let them be dissolved in their own waters until they are perfected.

<margin>4</margin> Take **quicklime** <note>original: *calcem vivum*; calcium oxide, a caustic substance</note> and place it in an iron vessel; put it over the fire and stir it until it turns red.

# Mercury

<margin>Note well</margin>
The power of this **Liquid** <note>original: *Liquoris*</note> no tongue could be strong enough to express, for it is prepared for the **poor** rather than the rich; if anyone knew the property of this liquid, they would truly never be poor again. It is a matter of the highest importance, for it **dissolves all metals** and reduces them to their **first matter** <term>first matter: *prima materia*, the original, formless substance from which alchemists believed all metals grew</term>, except for gold, for which reason it is to be worthily admired. **Take** <note>original: *℞*, the traditional recipe symbol for *Recipe*</note> the sharpest **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: distilled alcohol or ethanol</term> and **dissolving water of tartar** <note>original: *aqua solutiva de tartaro*; a solution derived from potassium bitartrate</note> in equal parts. Place them in a **retort** <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-curving neck used for distilling liquids over heat</term> over the fire for an hour, and distill through an **ash bath** <note>original: *per cineres*; using hot ashes to provide even, indirect heat</note> the liquid of the wine; then the spirit of wine will be sent from that part. Repeat this process with the received liquid twice. Afterward, extract the spirit of wine from the retort; in place of this spirit of wine, put in the sharpest spirit of mercury. **Lead, tin, heat, and plates of gold and silver** are dissolved in this liquid. Take care regarding this liquid, and it will be finished.

You will find in this liquid three parts: one is purified, the second is most pure, and the third consists of residues. From the residues, truly, the spirit of wine water is entirely distilled; the residue remains to be used in other metals. The spirit of wine returns to its former degree, quality, and weight. This **dissolved mercury** <note>original: *mercurius resolutus*</note> seems rather to be the concluding factor in this limit; I ask that you be diligent. Take 1 **pound** <note>original: *lib. j*</note> of sharp spirit of wine and 5 or 6 **drams** <note>original: *drach. v vel vj*</note> of **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," or nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</term>. Mix them and place them to be distilled through a retort, and that which is received, repeat over the dregs until it is finished. In this spirit, **mercury and sulfur** are dissolved; again, you will not be able to dissolve things in water otherwise than by such frequently repeated distillation. For the power of this liquid of wine is great, as it even **restores human life** <note>a reference to the "elixir of life"</note> and removes all corruption from metals. **Fixed water** <note>original: *aqua fixa*</note>. Spirit of wine of the third degree, a little **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux in chemistry</term> distilled through a retort; place it over the dregs of **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivi*</note>, and it receives the water which you will see purified when the spirits of wine are reduced in parts, and thus the mercury is finished for this water.

This is the **mystery of the spirit of wine and mercury**. Use only the retort here over the fire for four hours; the method of distilling the wine is the method described elsewhere. Take 1 pound of the best **white spirit of wine** and 1/2 pound 3 drams of **spirit of mercury**. Distill again through the retort as before, and you will receive the pure spirit of wine to make mercury, and again you will finish all parts of the metals; and that which is received, repeat over the remaining dissolved liquids to complete and conclude the work. Take 1/2 pound of the most powerful distilled spirit of wine, [and] 1 pound of spirit of mercury, water of life, and **oil of mercury**. It is a grace to both the poor and the rich because this is the **true mercury and the true sun** <note>original: *verum sol*; "Sun" is the alchemical symbol for Gold</note>, for it dissolves every metal; for this is a great mystery among all the mysteries of nature. Finish this in this spirit; it is recorded under this name elsewhere. <unclear>vlv 1596</unclear>.

Take 1/2 pound of the sharpest **rectified spirit of wine** and 1 pound of oil of mercury. Distill through a retort as above; this gives the **fixed spirit of mercury** and the most pure mercury for extracting its works—that is, for reducing all metals to their first matter. As you see, every body is dissolved into a liquid by this spirit of wine, powerful to this degree. Take 3 pounds of spirit of wine and 1 pound of spirit of mercury. Distill through a retort by the method of distillation, rather as you see. Here the **oil of wine** is dissolved in the spirit of mercury; in this spirit, you will be able to bring all metals to **perfect gold**, as was said before. Take 1/2 pound of the sharpest distilled spirit of wine, 1 pound of oil of wine, [and] 1/2 pound of aqua fortis. Place them for distillation as above, and this purges gold and silver and all metals. This is the **mercurial liquid** rather than all the mysteries to be sought by you regarding the method of the mercurial liquid; you see it under the name of **fixed mercury**. The end. This mystery of wine and mercury: repeat over the spirit of wine and finish this work of mercury according to the method you see elsewhere. Take 1 pound of spirit of wine and 1/2 pound of spirit of mercury. Distill through a retort for an hour, and this is mercury distilled and purified according to the method rather for **making gold**. Mercury is here recorded under the name of the **mystery of mercury and wine**. The end.

# On the Justice of God and Justification by Faith

...from sins: and so that he may wish his <term>justice</term> <note>original: *iustitiam*; in this context, it refers to "righteousness," the state of being right before God</note> to be shown, let him not despair; then at last he begins to groan and grieve over those things which he feels in himself to be without justice, and in this way he begins to become just: then he says, "I have sinned against you, Lord." And thus he shall be made just: + + + to show his justice. + that is, to show his Christ, through whom a person is <term>justified</term> <note>original: *iustificatur*; the process of being declared righteous or "cleansed" in a spiritual sense</note>: and thus God is not a liar, but just: and he shows himself to be just: because in no other way is a person made just unless God justifies the ungodly: Romans 3 and 4. And thus he makes us just through faith: and so he himself is just, and the one who justifies him who lives by the faith of Jesus Christ. In these words, he briefly and clearly shows the manner of justification and its effect, namely through his own justice and through his Christ: in whom we place our entire faith; and by faith, we are made healthy and saved before God. And because we are sinners: and we have nothing of good in ourselves except sin and misery: and therefore this faith and Christ are our justice. + + + + Therefore, in this state of the sinner who cannot deliver himself by his own strengths: Christ, the Son of God, came: who was made man for us: and died for us by the death of the cross: and through his blood, he atoned for our sins: and thus he reconciled us to God, that he might be made a Father to us: + + + + Thus you see, at last, the gift of the Holy Spirit, which is <term>charity</term> <note>original: *caritas*; here meaning divine, selfless love rather than mere modern "charity"</note>, given to us so that we may demonstrate our faith and live in him who suffered for us: through whom we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand and boast in the hope of the glory of the children of God: Romans 5. And thus love does not bring shame: because it has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us: + + + + as said above.

---

+ + + + Then it follows that the justice of God has been made manifest through faith and through Christ: through whom faith is justice to us: then God justifies the ungodly: and thus he shows himself to be just: by justifying those who are of faith: + + + + and thus it is clear that Christ is our justice: and that we have received all the gifts of God through him: justification, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and eternal life: so also in the same 5th chapter to the Romans it is said: "Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand: and we boast in the hope of the glory of God": + + + + and elsewhere in the same letter to the Romans, chapter 8, it is said: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus: who do not walk according to the flesh": + + + + and what follows: all of which teach that faith and Christ are necessary for us through all things and in all things: so that at last, through faith, we may be conformed to God: and in him our spirit may rest: and through the love of God, we may be made blessed. <meta>catchword: At last</meta>

---

...faith is not only conceived in this manner: which dwells in the mind and the intellect, but that which clings in the innermost chest <note>original: *pectore*; the heart or soul</note>: and from which, thereafter, true love and good works are born: this, I say, is the faith which justifies and makes a person whole; I call this the true [faith]: which is not only an assent regarding those things which are written or handed down in the Holy Scriptures: but which is true <term>trust</term> <note>original: *fiducia*; a key Reformation term distinguishing "heart-trust" from mere mental agreement</note> in the mercy of God: which is promised to us through Christ: this faith carries with it love and charity: for he does not confidently trust in the mercy of God, who did not a little while before love him: and from this follows joy: by which one becomes entirely cheerful toward God: then comes fear and shame for the sins conceived: for he who recognizes God and his love and grace toward himself cannot help but condemn himself: and from this is born <term>humility</term> <note>original: *humilitas*</note>: which is the foundation of all virtues: and which alone renders us acceptable in the sight of God: at last, let us conclude: because faith justifies: and Christ is our justice: and we have this living faith, which is not idle, but loving and eager. <meta>catchword: At last</meta>

It relies heavily on citations from the Book of Psalms and St. Gregory to explore the tension between human infirmity and divine power.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion of the "Highest Good" into a deeply mystical exploration of Divine Love (Agape). The author synthesizes Johannine theology with philosophical reflections on human relationships, arguing that the love shared between people is not merely a reflection of God, but the actual presence and "seeing" of God. The ink stain mentioned in the metadata obscures several verbs, but the repetitive, rhythmic nature of the prose allows for a confident reconstruction of the core argument.</meta>

...separates and brings back, so that among men the same memory of love <unclear>remains</unclear>. To see God whom they love—because God cannot be loved <unclear>manifestly</unclear> <note>meaning: "visibly" or "in His pure essence"</note> except only through receiving Him. As it is evident when beloved ones remember each other, the love they have for one another is evident, and they see that same love as God. As Moses says:

<margin>John</margin>

"No one can see God." <note>The author attributes the quote to Moses (likely referring to Exodus 33:20) but clarifies it through the lens of John the Apostle (1 John 4:12).</note> And again: "How can he love God, whom he has not seen?" He makes this manifest in the Epistle of John: that the love one has for another is the very seeing of God in that love. And how does he say that no one can see God? God resolves this: that the love one has for another is the seeing of God. As Solomon says: "As in water face reflects face, so the hearts of men reflect one another." <note>Proverbs 27:19; used here to suggest that we see God by looking into the heart of another through love.</note> For when one sees a beloved and they love them, and they remember that love which they have in themselves, they see that same God. For God is love. And how does <unclear>he say</unclear> that the heart remembers the beloved? Because the love that is in him sees that same God. For God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. And the beloved remain in God and God in them; therefore their hearts are one and their souls are one, for there is <unclear>one</unclear> God who dwells in them. And the love of God is one, <unclear>but</unclear> the beloved are many. And the love of God is one; and for those who love one another, that same love is the seeing of God.

<column-break/>

Ship, ship! <note>original: "նաւա նաւա" (*nawa nawa*); while this means "ship," in this mystical context it likely refers to the "Ship of the Church" or serves as a rhythmic liturgical refrain.</note> The cup reminds the servant of the heart; there, as a waking memory of love, he receives the same in various ways. When he begins to remember the creatures <note>meaning: all created beings</note> in God, he sends [into them] that which he names love, for the power of love is Love. The love of God is revealed in the midst of love, in the love of God; when <unclear>love</unclear> is there, when he sees himself sent into the love of God. For the love of God and our love for one another are mixed like water and wine with each other; in the same way, the love of God and our love are mixed as one. <note>The "water and wine" metaphor is a standard Christological and Eucharistic image, here applied to the union of human and divine affection.</note> For God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. And how is love called God? Because the love they have for one another is <unclear>one</unclear>, and the love God has for us is one. For love cannot separate God from itself, for love is God itself. And just as God is not separated from Himself, so also love is not separated from God. And those beloved of God are beloved of one another, for there is one God in them who loves them, and they love one another. And the love of God is manifest in those beloved of God, and the beloved of God are manifest in the love of God; for God is love. And how does it say that love is from God? It is clear that love is from God, because God is love, and love is from God. And those who love one another are born of God; for God is love, and love is from God. And whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him; for God is love, and love makes God manifest, and God makes love manifest. For they are one, like water and wine mixed together; therefore those beloved of God are one with God, and God is one with them; in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

<summary>This page presents a mystical treatise on the First Epistle of John, arguing that human love is the medium through which the invisible God becomes visible. It uses the metaphor of wine mixed with water to describe the inseparable union between divine love and brotherly affection.</summary>
<keywords>God is Love, Agape, mystical union, Epistle of John, Solomon, water and wine metaphor, divine indwelling, Notrgir script</keywords>

### Third Book of the Kabbalistic Wheels and the Names of Solomon: Concerning the Seven Names

1. The **First Name** is: the diamond of unity, which says: One God; because a demon can be worked upon by the weight [of this name]: and the demon having been poured in is immediately captured from there by this Name in the girdle of our under-shackles <note>This likely refers to a magical binding or containment ritual</note>, the name of which is Anetiephaphay.

<vocab>The End (Telos), symphony (simphonia), reason/proportion (ratio), union (unio), by much (multo), purged (purgato), in the deep (in profundo)</vocab>

<summary>This page presents a repetitive philosophical and quasi-musical discourse on the nature of spiritual "symphony" and "union" achieved through the divine names. It emphasizes that true union stands by itself through divine reason and proportion, moving between the "high" and the "deep."</summary>
<keywords>symphony, divine proportion, spiritual union, ritual purification, depth, height, Boethian harmony, Semiphoras</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Having detailed the divine names and numerical sequences of the Semiphoras on the previous page, the manuscript now shifts toward the practical and philosophical application of these powers within the art of alchemy. It explores how the "perfection" of materials is achieved through the tempering of substances like mercury and sulfur to reach the state of gold (Sol).</meta>

And because they say alchemy is of one species <note>original: "unius cum specie"; likely referring to the alchemical belief that all metals share a single underlying essence</note> which they hold in action, it is now in a state of perfection; but they then perfect it in such a way that it is not simply the sum of the earth in its own species. Another [aspect] is in nature: the tempering <term>tempering; the process of balancing the primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) of a substance</term> of the earth with the water of alchemy—the sum shall be perfected, though not by <unclear>nature</unclear>. Another is in matter: the material tempering, when they shall be perfected, not by <unclear>nature</unclear>, for matter can be instructed: led from the light out of the <unclear>expert</unclear> through the striking of alchemy. Since material things are said to be brought to this species through a period of time, through the earth, from a <unclear>partial</unclear> part of the sulfur in which there is so much mercury: although material things persuade this affection with all <unclear>clarity</unclear>, so that through the said tempering with the predicted perfection, this is accomplished—that is, the material [and] the moral sum of it: and then they persuade that it is material matter and moral matter <note>Alchemical "moral matter" likely refers to the "spirit" or "form" of the substance, as opposed to its physical "body" or material matter</note>. Two things which are perfected by perfection are here thoroughly imperfect; and they persuade through this, [it] is persuaded to be the matter of materials, to be the material matter of materials: in a material instrument. 

The other [aspect] is that matter can perceive the governance of sulfur: which is un-mergable, which proceeds. Material things are accomplished from alchemy from colors toward the perfect material: material to material, and so then material things, because the material is accomplished from alchemy only through colors. Material matter toward the perfect [state] through colors, so that it is material matter <unclear>...</unclear> the sum of colors is brought here. Since alchemy is perfected here through colors, so whence the material matter [is brought] to this instrument through colors. Of the color, it is that through those things, through this, the tempering of color is accomplished, always accomplished with the materials which through the material [attain] this material effect: the sum, the tempering of the color into gold <note>original: "aurum"</note> only through silver <note>original: "argentum"</note>, because the material [reaches] toward the perfect material matter in the Sun <note>original: "sole"; in alchemical shorthand, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold</note>; they are only the tempering of the Sun. And the perfection of the material matter [is] this Sun, perfected in the Sun: which [is] not through the material matter, but through this, perfected in the Sun; they are the tempering of sulfur in the Sun, accomplished in the Sun only. 

To this instrument of color through the Sun, this material matter is the tempering of the Sun. Another material matter through this accomplished material matter: the tempering in the Sun is accomplished. Another in the Sun is the tempering of the Sun; they are in colors, the tempering of the Sun. To this instrument of the Sun, accomplished through colors, they are the tempering of the Sun. Material matter [reaches] this accomplished material matter toward this instrument of the Sun. Another in the Sun is the tempering of the Sun, accomplished in this Sun toward this instrument. The Sun accomplished [is] material matter toward this instrument of colors; they are the tempering of the Sun. They are in colors, this Sun being accomplished, accomplished in the Sun; colors in the Sun, the Sun being accomplished. Having accomplished this material matter, the tempering of color in the Sun, they are the tempering of the Sun. And the perfection of material matter toward this instrument of the Sun; they are the colors of the Sun, they are the tempering of the Sun; and the perfection of material matter in the Sun, they are the tempering of the Sun. ...let it become a single **sublimate** <note>original: "sublimatum"; a solid substance produced by heating a material until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again upon cooling</note>. And after it has been sublimated, take that earth <note>the solid residue remaining in the flask</note> which was not sublimated and grind it; place it in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note> and upon it place that water which came out in the bath when it has stood for a day and a night, well-united and combined. Distill it again through an <term>alembic</term> <note>the "cap" or "hood" of a still that directs vapors into a cooling tube</note> and again place that water upon that earth and distill it again; and do this seven times. Do this until all that earth ascends through the alembic, and then it is done. And then you will have the **spirit of mercury** joined with water, and it will be a thing of great value, and then you will have that water for wonderful and very powerful things.

Furthermore, another way by which a valuable **oil** is made:
take prepared common salt by means of that "water of the earths" and place it in a cucurbit, and then distill through an alembic, and you will have a precious oil for doing many things.

Furthermore, another way by which **mercury water** is made:
take 1 pound <note>original: "lb i."</note> of Roman <term>vitriol</term> <note>likely copper or iron sulfate</note> and 4 ounces <note>original: "oz iiij"</note> of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>; let them be ground separately and mixed; then distill through an alembic and you will have mercurial water.

Furthermore, it can be made another way:
take sal ammoniac, sulfur, frankincense, and raw mercury; let them be mixed and distill through an alembic and you will have it.

Furthermore, another way of preparing **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>:
take <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate</note> and Roman vitriol, 1 pound of each, and <unclear>let them be ground</unclear> <unclear>well</unclear> and mixed; then place them in a cucurbit and place water upon them and distill through an alembic; you will then have the **spirit of saltpeter** <note>this process likely produced a diluted nitric acid</note> <unclear>with</unclear> <unclear>which</unclear> <unclear>silver</unclear> <note>original: "luna"; the alchemical name for silver</note> <unclear>is dissolved</unclear>.

<summary>This page contains a highly repetitive and fragmented philosophical discussion on the "virtues" of mercury and silver (Luna), focusing on the processes of calcination and the use of aqua fortis to achieve the stage of albedo (whiteness). The marginal note and main text emphasize the self-perfecting nature of these alchemical substances when combined with spirits of salt and sulfur.</summary>

<margin>a</margin>
Only two things of <unclear>nature</unclear> should it have, because medicinal things are found by nature through which fire is found, and that fire is but from the resolved fire. The fire is for the fire through the "head" <note>original: "caput"; likely refers to the "caput mortuum" or the dregs left after distillation</note> in the fire of the powder, from the added **hot water**. Then, and rather, pour <note>original: "funde"; can mean to pour, melt, or establish a foundation</note> this fire from these by heat alone, and it overcomes. To bring to the fire, it overcomes this fire in the pouring. It is almost in vain; that is, nothing can be preserved from it because it is fire—that is, otherwise the color could not be similar to human blood, even in the color of the fire. Otherwise, it is rather through this that the fire then can resolve into another.

<margin>b</margin>
**Sulphur** in the work has that which is effective by its own nature, which you will desire through the intervention of the white spirit. The humid spirit, the extreme of existing liquids from the humid, and from the stone through fire. With the water following in the month of May <note>Alchemists often collected "May dew," believing it contained a celestial spirit or "universal solvent" needed for the Great Work</note>, it is possible what was not elsewhere. And through bringing heat, through pouring, through those things it overcomes. Through pouring, that is through the spirit through which the stone desires—that is, it is resolved. That is, pour; that is, through that [spirit] of sulphur in the fire, or rather, in this that is through fire. That is, through the spirit; that is, through the various stages. In this, in its own way, through our **Sulphur**, which is fixed, which is dissolved through fire. The spirit by itself without the "sun" <note>original: "sole"; refers to gold or the masculine principle</note> will be conquered; that is, and it will not be hot. That is the spirit; that is, according to my water, fire for fire; that is, fire for fire.

<summary>This page presents a Scholastic philosophical argument on hylomorphism, debating whether the soul is merely a "form" of the body or a "subsistent thing" (hoc aliquid) that can exist by itself. The author concludes that while the soul is the form of the body, it retains its own being, and it is the union of the two that constitutes the individual human person.</summary>
<keywords>soul, body, form, matter, hylomorphism, essence, subsistence, Aristotle, Scholasticism, rational soul</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page's instructions on preparing metallic solutions and 'calx' using spirit of wine, this page transitions into a theoretical and practical discussion on the "virtue" or active power found in honey, wine, and water through the processes of boiling and distillation.</meta>

<margin>☿ 🜍 🜔</margin> <note>These are alchemical symbols for Mercury, Sulfur, and likely Salt or Water, representing the foundational principles of matter.</note>

# Chapter on Rue
<margin>+</margin>Pennyroyal <note>original: "pulegio"</note> is very effective against the plague and against poison. Take rue <note>original: "rutas"</note> and pennyroyal and pound them together; drink this with wine and it shall save you from death. Also, if anyone chews rue, it is effective against poison. Also, the juice of rue drunk with wine is effective against the bite of a serpent. Also, rue pounded with honey and salt is effective against scabies <note>a contagious skin infestation causing intense itching</note> and against pains of the kidneys. Also, if anyone chews rue before the onset of a fever, it is effective against the fever. Also, mint and rue are effective for clear eyes if they are drunk pounded with water, and they are even more effective if drunk with wine. Also, mint pounded with vinegar and pepper is effective against catarrh <note>excessive buildup of mucus</note> of the head and against a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>. Also, if anyone chews mint, it is effective for toothache. Also, mint with honey-water <note>original: "aqua mulsa," a mixture of water and honey</note> is effective against a cough. Also, mint pounded with salt and honey is effective against the poison of a serpent. Also, mint with water is effective against the bite of a rabid dog.

# Chapter on Mint
Mint is hot and dry in the second degree <term>degrees: a system in Galenic medicine used to measure the intensity of a plant's "humoral" qualities</term>. Mint is effective against stomach worms. Also, mint is effective against stomach pain and against vomiting. Also, if anyone chews mint with salt and vinegar, it is effective against toothache. Also, mint with honey-water is effective against a cough. Also, mint pounded with salt and honey is effective against the poison of a serpent. Also, mint with water is effective against the bite of a rabid dog. Also, the juice of mint smeared on with honey is effective against abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note> of the ears. Also, if anyone chews mint and places it over the bite of a rabid dog, it is very effective. Also, if anyone drinks mint with water, it is effective against a flux of the belly. Also, mint with honey-water is effective against a cough. Also, mint pounded with salt is effective against the poison of a serpent. Also, mint is effective against fevers and against all pains of the stomach. Also, if anyone drinks mint with honey-water, it is effective against a cough. Also, mint pounded with salt is effective against the poison of a serpent.

Also, pennyroyal pounded and smeared on is effective against abscesses and headache. Also, if one eats it with salt and pepper, it is effective against stomach pain. Also, pennyroyal pounded and smeared on with vinegar is effective against scabies. Also, if anyone drinks pennyroyal with water, it is effective against pain of the kidneys. Also, pennyroyal dried and powdered and eaten with salt and pepper is effective against a long-standing cough. Also, if anyone rubs on pennyroyal pounded with honey, it is effective against "suffocation of the mother" <term>suffocation of the mother: a historical term for a hysterical or respiratory condition believed to be caused by the womb moving upward in the body</term>. # Chapter 4: On the Cough
For a cough, the roots of nettle <note>original: "urtice"</note> pounded with wine and drunk are effective. Also, nettle seed with honey is very effective. Also, if anyone chews nettle with pepper, it is effective for a cough. Also, a decoction of nettle with honey smeared on the throat is effective for a cough. Also, if you drink nettle with honey-water, it is effective against a cough. Also, the juice of nettle pounded with salt is effective against jaundice. Also, if anyone boils nettle with oil and anoints the joints, it is very effective. Also, nettle is effective against swelling of the testicles.

---

# Chapter 5: On Fevers
For a daily fever <note>original: "febre cotidianam," a fever that recurs every day</note>, let the juice of centaury <note>original: "centauree"</note> be taken with hot water. Also, the juice of horehound <note>original: "marubii"</note> is effective against fevers. Also, the juice of wormwood <note>original: "absintii"</note> with wine is effective against fevers. Also, the juice of rue with wine is effective against fevers. Also, if anyone carries the root of celery <note>original: "api"</note> with them, it is effective against fevers. Also, it is effective if anyone chews the root of celery with wine before the onset of the fever. Also, the root of plantain <note>original: "plantaginis"</note> with water is effective. Also, the juice of vervain <note>original: "verbene"</note> drunk with hot water is effective. Also, if anyone washes their feet and hands before the onset of the fever, it is very effective.

---

### For a Tertian Fever
Take three leaves of plantain and pound them and distill them with wine and water and give it to be drunk before the onset <note>of the fever</note>. Also, three leaves of plantain pounded with wine and drunk are effective. Also, if anyone carries vervain with them before the onset, it is effective.

---

### For a Quartan Fever
Take four leaves of plantain and pound them with wine and let them be drunk. Also, the roots of parsley <note>original: "petrosilini"</note> pounded with wine and drunk are effective. Also, it is effective if you drink the juice of wild thyme <note>original: "serpilli"</note> mixed with water and vinegar. Also, if you drink the juice of rue with salt and water.

---

# For Burning Water
Take a vessel <note>original: "iustam"</note> of [good] color and let a little heat be applied. Also, take good wine; it is effective for fevers. Also, if it is made from strong wine it is better, and it should be taken while facing the sun. Also, it strengthens the sight and the memory. Also, it is effective for all wounds and the bites of serpents. Also, it is effective if anyone anoints themselves with it. And if anyone drinks it, it is effective for [an unclear purpose] because it provokes urine and menstruation. Also, it is effective against scabies. Also, it purges the body of slime and melancholy <term>melancholy: one of the four humors, associated with "black bile" and thought to cause sadness or sluggishness if in excess</term>. Also, it is effective against all pains of the body and creates a good complexion. Also, it is effective if wounds are washed with it. Also, if anyone drinks it, they escape drunkenness <note>possibly meaning it cures a hangover or prevents intoxication</note>. Also, it is effective against toothache if one washes with it. And if anyone carries it with them, <unclear>fessa</unclear> flee. It is proven. Moreover, it is best to make this on the 15th day of June or in the months of May and June when [the herbs] are in their flowers. Also, you should take four pounds of wine and decant it with burning water <note>original: "aquam ardente," likely brandy or distilled spirits</note>. And if you wish to make it good instead of very poor, it is better if the <unclear>le</unclear> solution is made two or three times, and it will always be better; and let it be done through an instrument for distilling <note>an alembic</note>. It is proven.

# Receipt of the much useful fourth book of Geber’s alchemical antidotes:

## ¶ For fixing sal ammoniac

Take <note>original: "F. cap^o"; likely a contraction of "Recipe" or "Capiat," meaning "Take"</note> 2 parts. 1. Let it suffer in solution and 3 parts sal ammoniac <note>original: "sal armoniaci"; ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used to clean metals</note>. Let there be earths and through those let it be suspended: above the water: after it is cooked: you place 2 parts water of sal ammoniac. Heat for one day in the mixed earth in white <note>original: "in albua"; likely referring to the *albedo* or whitening stage of alchemy</note>: when it has become a paste: and good and shining: and dried: as if by human leisure: without the drying of God into black: afterwards let it be well cleaned. 3 parts. as hard as alum glaze. Salt in winter water. Earth in water. in 1 part earth strained 3 parts in 1 part of salt as prepared as this preparation. Afterwards in winter: and dry: after these things prepare this. just as in white earth in the water of the earth the part of the earth lasts. you place in that "Vincent" <note>possibly a reference to a specific alchemical authority or a specific substance name</note>: after it breathes: take the mixture in the vessel: until this is made. The earth of Vincent: by heating.

## ¶ For fixing Sal ammoniac:

Take sal ammoniac. ### Solution of sulfur by the fixed substance ###

Take and dissolve with one fermented water of earth <note>original: "fermentā t̄re"; likely referring to a mineral-based solvent or "water of the philosopher's earth"</note> and give of the red <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: 🜍; the active, combustible principle in alchemy</note> residue. Then, through the tincture, grind by half and give of the red sulfur where the water has lost its strength. And then you [make] the salt of the apples <note>original: "sal poma"; possibly referring to a crystalline structure resembling fruit or a specific alchemical code</note>. Let it be made.

### All sulfur by itself ###

Dissolve the residue in fresh water, filter it, and then wash this red [substance]. Likewise, as before, dissolve again through the tincture; after this, twice by weight, let the water be made by itself. Give of the earth as long as it is required. Let it be made.

### Oil of sulfur by the fixed substance ###

Take of the water as much as is found of sulfur, and let it dissolve slowly. Then let it be <term>luted</term> <note>original: "lūter"; sealed with "lute," a clay or cement used to make vessels airtight</note> in a glass vessel for a day's fermentation of the earth. That which is said to be made, let it be given from the water of sulfur in a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cupello"; a porous vessel used to separate precious metals from lead and other impurities</note> so that it descends. Then you will save it and it will go clearly to the bottom; removing it afterward, let it be placed to descend together. Let it be made where you will save it and where you have hoped for it again. Let it be luted in a vessel together; this shall be done while it is sent within; then let it be done.

### Fixation of sulfur by the fixed substance ###

Take a sufficient quantity with waters, and let this [amount] come to be made as much as is required. While it is sent into you, place in this earth again for a certain day, and while it is able, let it be given. And this is not to be added: the water [reacts] as the book says, the waters are made. Let it be made.

### Fixation for the portion of fixed things ###

Take of the red [substance] while it wishes to go to its own red [parts]. All humidity, while it wishes to be a red powder, comes to be made again while you [hold] this in the light for three days, remaining in the bottom.

### Fixation of the water in which Mercury is ###

### To the same again ###

Take this water in the first water of the flux where the living sulfur is made. While the earth is broken, this earth [becomes] a red powder through the water, while it gives and the red is made. And because it gives this through the earth, while there is as much sulfur as there is water, and as much earth as there is <term>mercury</term> <note>original: ☿; also known as "argentum vivum," representing the principle of volatility</note>, let it be made for those to whom the water returns for a day of light, while this is produced from the first waters. And then it is best when it is made, while it falls into the white <note>original: "albū"; referring to the 'albedo' or whitening stage of the alchemical process</note> and remains. Let it be made.

### A beautiful whiteness and fixation ###

Take while it falls, send it while it is in the light. This gives the red, the red salt is broken. Afterward, send water upon the red salt, as much as is needed. Send the powder, let it be made. While it is joined, while the earth is given from the red powder.

### Fixation of the cupel ###

Give the red, send the red of the earth. Let the water of the earth be made, while the water of the fixed salt of sulfur is made. The water of the red [substance] is sent again, and from the water the earth is sent. The humidity remains, and this.

## To make a thief stop in his tracks
Take dust from beneath your feet and say seven times over the dust: <note>original: "leuaui oculos meos ad montes"</note> *I lifted up my eyes to the mountains* until help comes to me. Also say your song. Then, throw part of the dust behind your back over your head, and throw the other part in the face of the one you suspect. In this way, he will not move.

## A sign to strengthen you in judgment.
Write upon the lips <note>original: "per labres in labiis"</note> that which is said therein, until it creates a judgment through the lips in your favor. It shall renew your mouth to our [advantage].

## If you wish to be freed from prison.
Say seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "confitebor tibi domine"</note> *I will confess to you, O Lord* over all our [need], until he brings you out of prison. And write this Psalm and tie it under your arm; it is said that he who is in prison shall be freed or let go.

## To be enlightened and loved by adversaries above all others.
Say on any day seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "domine probasti me"</note> *O Lord, you have searched me*, and [say] to me, O Lord: you shall be a kind son.

## To be favored in matters of love.
Say seven times into your hand and seven times into your mouth the Psalm, until [you reach the words] *call me*, and it shall appear under my lips [as] my prayer to the Lord most high for me; and let it be bound.

## So that nothing harms you on a journey.
Whenever you are at home, say to the Lord seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "domine clamaui ad te"</note> *O Lord, I have cried out to you*; then go securely, and nothing [evil] shall happen.

## That God may free one from prison.
Say seven times in the morning and seven times in the evening: <note>original: "uoce mea ad dominum clamaui"</note> *With my voice I cried out to the Lord*, until our adversaries are no longer seen, and you shall be freed.

## That God may make you win in judgment.
Write the Psalm <note>original: "uoce mea ad dominum"</note> *With my voice [I cried] to the Lord*, and he hears; then tie it upon your right foot, and it shall be so.

## To prevent someone from being burned in fire or mourning.
Say seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "domino laus omnium meum"</note> *Praise of the Lord is all mine*, until the abundance of my weakness [is gone], and be freed by the names; and you shall be restored.

## That someone may lose to his enemy in a game.
When you wish for an enemy to lose, say seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "laudate dominum deum meum"</note> *Praise the Lord my God*, and he shall conquer his weaknesses. Write this upon a heart <note>This may refer to a heart-shaped piece of parchment or a specific gaming token.</note> for the enemy and carry it with you.

## Against a sea storm

## So that no words proceed against someone.
Say seven times into your hand the Psalm: <note>original: "laudate dominum deum super omnem bonum"</note> *Praise the Lord God above every good thing*, and until it reaches the head, throw the dirt, and let him hold the hem of his garment by the arm, and his face shall return to his [original] intention.

## To be preserved and seen [favorably] in a legal process.
Say seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "laudat te domine super omnem bonum"</note> *The Lord praises you above every good thing*, and [until the verse] *of the weak*, and let his word be praised.

## And for achieving victory.
Say seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "lauda anima mea dominum"</note> *Praise the Lord, O my soul*, until [the verse] *the Lord rules others*, and until this is finished, you shall rejoice.

## For making peace.
Say the Psalm: <note>original: "laudate dominum quoniam bonus est"</note> *Praise the Lord for he is good*. Say the Psalm *Praise the Lord* until someone is in trade [at peace], and until [the verse] *of the weak*, and you shall rejoice.

## To assist in childbirth through a woman.
If you wish for someone to give birth with another [help] and she is not able to do so, say seven times the Psalm: <note>original: "laudate dominum de celis"</note> *Praise the Lord from the heavens* <note>Psalm 148</note>, until she is seen to be giving birth; then gather the [afterbirth/part] by hand and let her labor.

### On quicksilver in perfect vitriol:

Take 1 pound of citrine silver <note>original: "argento citrino"; likely silver that has been chemically treated to appear yellow or "citrine"</note>, 2 pounds of Armenian bole <note>A red medicinal clay often used as a base in alchemical mixtures</note>, 1 pound of cinnabar <note>A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide</note>, and 3 pounds of iron. Grind every thing very well individually; then mix them together to make a paste. Dry it in the sun. Then place it in a "ball of lute" <note>A protective lump of sealing clay or cement</note> and put the fire in the furnace where lead is smelted. Then take the said silver and cupel it <note>A process of refining precious metals in a shallow, porous cup</note> with 1 pound and <unclear>...</unclear> of tutty <note>A crude zinc oxide residue from smelting</note> and 2 ounces of the same bread. This makes beautiful gold again.
